tannin: High — firm, "gripping," felt on the gums; ages into smoother, more integrated tannin over years
acidity: Medium to high
sweetness: Dry
finish: Long
colour: Deep ruby to garnet — one of the deepest of any red grape, from thick skins
primaryAroma: Black currant (cassis), black cherry, blackberry, plum; a distinctive green bell pepper note especially in cooler-climate/less-ripe examples (methoxypyrazines)
secondaryTertiary: Vanilla, clove, baking spice, cedar from oak aging; with bottle age: tobacco, leather, graphite
styleRange: One dominant style (full-bodied, structured, built to age), with a real Old World/New World split: Bordeaux tends more herbal/graphite/tobacco with more pronounced green pepper; Napa and other New World examples tend riper, more fruit-forward, higher ABV, softer green notes
confusedWithNote: Merlot — Cabernet’s tannin feels firmer/more angular and grips the sides of the mouth; Merlot’s is rounder, softer, "plush." Secondary: Syrah/Shiraz — Cabernet’s acid runs higher and tannin more angular; Syrah is rounder-tannined with a black pepper note (rotundone) that roughly 1 in 10 people cannot smell at all
globalPrevalence: World’s #1 most-planted wine grape variety, ~341,000 hectares, roughly 5% of total world vineyard area (OIV Focus 2017)
foodPairing: Complement — its high tannin wants fat (red meat, aged hard cheese) to soften against

tannin: Low to medium — texture is the real signature: "silky," "soft," "fine-grained," a genuinely different feel from a grippy red, not just a lower amount of the same feel
acidity: High, sometimes described as the grape’s single defining trait
sweetness: Dry
abv: 12–14.5% (cooler regions 12–13.5%; warmer New World regions run higher within the band)
finish: Medium, elegant rather than powerful
colour: Pale ruby to bright ruby-red — one of the lightest-coloured red wines, from thin skins
primaryAroma: Red cherry, raspberry, strawberry, cranberry; floral notes (violet, rose)
secondaryTertiary: Vanilla/spice from modest oak use (rarely 100% new oak); with age: mushroom, forest floor, leather, game, truffle
styleRange: Narrower than Riesling’s — always dry, always relatively light — but aroma shifts noticeably: young Pinot is fresh red fruit, aged Pinot moves toward dried fruit and earthy/savoury tertiary notes. Climate matters more for texture/weight than for a dry-sweet axis
confusedWithNote: Gamay (not a full entry in this file) — a genetic relative (natural cross of Pinot Noir × Gouais Blanc), sharing light body, high acid, low tannin; Gamay is more overtly floral/candied, Pinot shows more structure and earthiness. Secondary, per the Tim Gaiser "Evil Dwarves" red cluster: Nebbiolo (not a full entry here), told apart bluntly — Nebbiolo’s tannin and acid both run considerably higher. Also a genetic parent (cross) of Chardonnay and, via colour mutation through Pinot Gris, ancestor of Pinot Blanc — a real lineage fact, not a taste pairing
globalPrevalence: Ranks around #9 among the world’s most-planted grape varieties, roughly 115,000 hectares (OIV-sourced ranking table; ranking position well-sourced, exact hectare figure less independently cross-checked)
foodPairing: Complement, but unusually flexible for a red — low tannin and high acid let it pair like a food-friendly white would (salmon, mushroom dishes, roast chicken), not just red meat

tannin: None (white grape)
acidity: Very high — consistently one of the highest-acid grapes made into wine at any real volume
sweetness: Genuinely spans bone-dry to intensely sweet, not a fixed point — a winemaking decision, not something inherent to the grape
abv: Inverse to sweetness: roughly 12–14% for dry styles, dropping to 7–9% for the sweetest styles, since less sugar is fermented into alcohol the sweeter the target style
finish: Long — the high acidity gives Riesling unusually strong aging potential even at low alcohol
colour: Very pale, often with a slight green tinge when young
primaryAroma: Green apple, lime, lemon, grapefruit in cooler/drier styles; peach, apricot, tropical fruit in riper/warmer styles; floral notes (honeysuckle, jasmine, orange blossom) throughout
secondaryTertiary: Petrol/kerosene/diesel aroma on aging — caused by TDN (1,1,6-trimethyl-1,2-dihydronaphthalene), forming from carotenoid precursors via acid-driven hydrolysis during bottle aging, intensified by vineyard sun exposure. Peer-reviewed sensory threshold ~2 µg/L; aged examples can reach 50+
styleRange: The defining trait of this grape: spans bone-dry (Trocken, Wachau’s Smaragd tier) through off-dry (Kabinett, Spätlese) to intensely sweet (Auslese, Beerenauslese, ice wine). Determined by harvest timing/ripeness and a winemaking choice about how much fermentation runs before being stopped, not a fixed grape character
confusedWithNote: Chenin Blanc — the closest real analogue, the only other major white with a genuinely comparable dry-to-sweet range and comparably high acid; Chenin carries a waxy/lanolin note and more phenolic weight, Riesling shows the petrol/TDN note and typically the highest extract of the two. Secondary, per the "Evil Dwarves" white cluster: Grüner Veltliner, distinguished by GV’s white-pepper/vegetal note that dry Riesling lacks
globalPrevalence: No exact number found. Not in the world top-10 by hectares the way the other Tranche 1 grapes are — Germany’s own most-planted grape, but Germany’s total vineyard area is modest by world standards; a global figure comparable to the OIV top-10 table was not located
foodPairing: Contrast — high acidity and (in off-dry/sweet styles) sweetness classically cut through rich, fatty, or spicy food rather than mirror it

body: Medium, trending toward medium-full in more serious expressions (Brunello di Montalcino fuller-bodied than everyday Chianti)
tannin: Medium to high — firm; several sources specifically describe the texture as "chalky," "dusty," or "powdery" rather than the smoother grip other high-tannin reds show
acidity: High — several sources note acidity is usually more pronounced than the tannin, i.e. the more immediately obvious structural feature on tasting
sweetness: Dry
abv: 11.5–14% (Chianti tends lower-middle; Brunello, aged 4+ years minimum from a specific clone, runs higher)
finish: Medium to long, especially in Riserva/Brunello-level examples
colour: Ruby-garnet, holding colour longer with age than some other thin-skinned Italian reds (see Nebbiolo comparison)
primaryAroma: Sour/tart red cherry, red plum, cranberry; a distinctive tomato leaf note recurring across enough independent sources to count as a real varietal marker
secondaryTertiary: Dried herbs, violet (young); leather, tobacco, balsamic, dried fruit, truffle-like earthiness (aged, especially Brunello); vanilla/cedar with oak use
styleRange: Real but narrower than Riesling’s: always dry, but spans lighter/fresher stainless-steel styles (Rosso di Montalcino, everyday Chianti) through powerful, tannic, age-worthy Brunello — determined mainly by DOCG-level rules (yield limits, minimum aging) and winemaking choice rather than harvest-timing
confusedWithNote: Nebbiolo (not a full entry here) — explicitly termed "wine twins" by a named professional source (David Glancy MS, CWE); the most reliable tell is a counterintuitive colour/tannin mismatch — Nebbiolo looks deceptively pale and translucent (even paler than Sangiovese) but carries the more formidable, longer-aging tannin of the two. Aroma-wise, Nebbiolo leans tar/rose/licorice while Sangiovese leans tomato-leaf/violet/sour cherry. Secondary, per the "Evil Dwarves" cluster: Gamay, told apart mainly by carbonic-maceration bubblegum-like notes in Gamay that Sangiovese doesn’t show
globalPrevalence: Italy’s single most-planted grape variety, though still doesn’t exceed roughly 8% of Italy’s own total vineyard area — a useful corrective against assuming "most planted in Italy" means globally dominant
foodPairing: Complement — high acidity is specifically built for tomato-based dishes (the acid matches the tomato’s own acid rather than clashing), the textbook reason Chianti-and-red-sauce is such a stock pairing

tannin: None (white grape)
acidity: High to very high — one of the most reliably acidic major white grapes
sweetness: Typically dry; a real minority of commercial/entry-level examples carry a touch of residual sugar specifically to balance very high acidity, but this is a winemaking choice at the margins, not a real style range
finish: Medium — bright and tart rather than long and powerful
colour: Very pale, often with a distinct green-tinted cast
primaryAroma: Two distinct, chemically-named aroma families: green/herbaceous (cut grass, green bell pepper, gooseberry, asparagus, tomato leaf) from methoxypyrazines; and tropical/citrus (passionfruit, guava, grapefruit, lime) from volatile thiols, notably 4-MMP. Which dominates depends on climate/ripeness at harvest — cooler/less ripe leans green, warmer/riper leans tropical
secondaryTertiary: Usually minimal — most often made in stainless steel specifically to preserve the primary aroma character; a minority (some White Bordeaux, blended with Sémillon) age in oak for a rounder, waxier, creamier style, a real but distinctly minority expression
styleRange: Narrower than Riesling’s — always dry-leaning, always high acid — but with a real regional-style axis: Loire Valley (Sancerre/Pouilly-Fumé) tends restrained, mineral, green-leaning; Marlborough tends louder, more overtly tropical/thiol-driven; both are equally "correct" expressions, not a quality gradient
confusedWithNote: Verdejo (Rueda, Spain, not a full entry here) — the closest real-world lookalike, close enough that Spanish law allows the two to be blended under the same Rueda DO designation. Secondary: Grüner Veltliner, sharing high acid and green/vegetal lean but showing a more overtly white-peppery, sometimes nutty character and less tropical-thiol lift
globalPrevalence: Ranks around #8 among the world’s most-planted grape varieties, roughly 121,000 hectares (conservative end of a 121,000–123,000 range; OIV Focus 2017, cross-checked against a second independent citation)
foodPairing: Contrast, classically — high acid and green/herbal notes are the textbook pairing for goat cheese, oysters, and green vegetable-forward dishes that would clash with a rounder, lower-acid white

tannin: Medium — recurring texture language is "soft," "velvety," "plush," directly confirming the same contrast already named from Cabernet Sauvignon’s own side
acidity: Medium (one source said "low," most converge on "medium" — treated as normal source variance)
sweetness: Dry
finish: Medium to long
colour: Deep ruby-purple, generally a shade lighter than Cabernet Sauvignon
primaryAroma: Black cherry, plum, black currant, raspberry
secondaryTertiary: Vanilla, cocoa, baking spice from oak; with age moves toward leather, tobacco, dried fruit
styleRange: One dominant style (soft, plush, approachable), with the same cool-vs-warm-climate axis as Cabernet: cooler sites (Right Bank Bordeaux, Languedoc) show more herbal/earthy character and firmer tannin; warmer New World sites show riper, rounder, more fruit-forward expression
confusedWithNote: Cabernet Sauvignon — already established from the opposite direction. The tell: structure over fruit — Merlot’s tannin is rounder/softer/"plush," Cabernet’s is firmer/more angular and grips the sides of the mouth
globalPrevalence: World’s #2 most-planted wine grape, ~266,000 hectares (OIV Focus 2017-lineage data)
foodPairing: Complement — softer tannin than Cabernet makes it more broadly food-friendly, still pairs with red meat and firm cheese but doesn’t need as much fat to soften against

body: Genuinely bimodal: light-to-medium (unoaked/cool-climate) or medium-to-full (oaked/warm-climate) — the single defining fact of this entry
tannin: None (white grape) — a very small minority of heavily-oaked styles can show a faint "grip" from oak tannin itself, not the grape
acidity: High (unoaked/cool-climate) to medium (oaked/warm-climate, softened further by malolactic fermentation)
sweetness: Dry, always — but oak-driven vanilla/toast aromas can read as "sweet" to an untrained palate with zero actual residual sugar
finish: Medium; savory/creamy on the finish specifically in oaked styles
colour: Medium straw to deep gold depending on style; unoaked skews paler/greener, oaked skews deeper gold
primaryAroma: Green apple, lemon, lime (unoaked/cool-climate) or peach, pineapple, mango (oaked/warm-climate) — Chardonnay is repeatedly described as a "neutral" grape with muted inherent aroma; character is a winemaking decision far more than a grape-inherent trait
secondaryTertiary: Vanilla, butter, toast, coconut, baking spice from oak and malolactic fermentation; the dominant character in "oaked" styles, essentially absent in unoaked/stainless-steel styles. With age, hazelnut aromas develop regardless of oak use
styleRange: Chardonnay’s range is almost entirely a winemaking decision layered onto a genuinely neutral base grape — stainless steel vs. oak, with or without malolactic fermentation. Same grape, two near-opposite finished wines, by choice rather than terroir alone
confusedWithNote: Viognier (not a full entry here) — both full-bodied, often-oaked whites, genuinely challenging to tell apart blind. Chardonnay is "explosive on the attack" with a savory/creamy finish; Viognier has a famously "oily/glycerol" texture and a floral/tangerine perfumed lift Chardonnay generally lacks. Minor: unoaked Chardonnay is sometimes compared to Pinot Grigio/Sauvignon Blanc-adjacent territory, precisely because the grape’s neutral character leaves little to distinguish it once oak is removed
globalPrevalence: World’s #5 most-planted wine grape overall and #1 among white grapes specifically (surpassing Airén around 2010), ~211,000 hectares
foodPairing: Flexible — oaked styles complement richer dishes (roast poultry, cream sauces) the way a red would; unoaked styles work more by contrast (shellfish, light fish)

tannin: Medium to high — most sources converge on "medium-plus" to "high"; firm but not harsh, softening further with extended oak aging
acidity: Moderate — with a specific, repeated descriptor: "citrusy" or "orange-peel-like" acidity, distinct from a generic "high acid" claim
sweetness: Dry
finish: Medium to long, smooth, often with tannin lingering on both sides of the mouth
colour: Ruby-red when young, shifting to garnet/ruddy-orange with age and traditional Spanish oak aging
primaryAroma: Black cherry, plum, red berries; a genuinely distinctive tomato/dried-tomato note recurs across sources, echoing (independently) Sangiovese’s own tomato-leaf marker
secondaryTertiary: Dill, vanilla, leather, tobacco, cedar, clove — tightly tied to Rioja’s aging-classification system (Joven = little/no oak; Crianza = 1+ year oak; Reserva = 1+ year oak plus bottle age; Gran Reserva = 2+ years oak plus extended bottle age)
styleRange: Largely a function of the oak-aging classification system above — a Joven shows bright unoaked fruit, a Gran Reserva shows the full secondary/tertiary oak-driven profile. Also a real regional split independent of oak: Rioja tends elegant/balanced, Ribera del Duero and Toro (more extreme continental climates) tend powerful/higher-alcohol/darker-fruited
confusedWithNote: Sangiovese — confirmed via the Tim Gaiser MS "Evil Dwarves" red cluster and independently corroborated by a hands-on blind-tasting account. Gaiser’s tell: Tempranillo’s American-oak-driven signature (coconut, dill, pronounced vanilla, baking spice) most reliably separates it from Sangiovese, Nebbiolo, and Pinot Noir. Independent corroboration: Tempranillo read as "more muted and earthy," Sangiovese as "more savory/sour, sour tomato character"
globalPrevalence: World’s #3 most-planted wine grape, ~231,000 hectares; over 80% of world plantings are in Spain itself
foodPairing: Complement — structure and savory oak-driven notes pair with roasted/grilled meats and firm cheeses; also a good match with Mexican cuisine

tannin: Medium, though multiple sources specifically note it reads as softer/rounder than the level alone would suggest
acidity: Genuinely bidirectional depending on region: Cahors consistently higher-acid/structured; Mendoza consistently lower-acid/softer — closer to two distinct wine identities under one grape name than a simple gradient
sweetness: Dry
abv: 13–15%, with Mendoza examples common above 14% given the region’s hot climate
finish: Notably shorter than Cabernet Sauvignon or Merlot per one direct source comparison
colour: Deep purple to inky black — among the darkest of any major red grape; a distinctive "magenta rim," specific enough to be named as a blind-tasting marker
primaryAroma: Black plum, blackberry, black cherry, violet
secondaryTertiary: Cocoa, vanilla, sweet tobacco, coffee/mocha from oak — Mendoza examples typically see less oak time (6–10 months) than Old World norms, letting fruit character dominate more than oak character
styleRange: A real, pronounced, region-driven split. Cahors (cooler, limestone): structured, earthy, savory, higher acid, firmer tannin, red-fruit-leaning. Mendoza (hot, high-altitude): plush, soft, generous, lower acid, rounder tannin, dark-fruit-leaning. Altitude specifically (not just latitude) is repeatedly cited as the key factor preserving acidity in Mendoza’s warm climate
confusedWithNote: Genuinely weaker than most confused-with pairings in this file — flagged explicitly rather than presented at equal confidence. Syrah/Shiraz is the closest real pairing, but multiple sources (including a direct forum discussion among actual tasters) call it more a casual-consumer-level lumping-together than a genuine tasting-exam-level confusion; several tasters say they don’t find the two similar on close tasting. Where a real tell is given: Syrah/Shiraz shows black pepper and smoke that Malbec lacks; Malbec is purer/plusher fruit with more floral lift. Separately, "Malbec argenté" is a different grape entirely (Abouriou), a name-confusion not a taste-confusion
globalPrevalence: Argentina holds roughly 75% of world Malbec plantings (well-converged). Argentina’s own most recent figure (~47,000 ha, ~23% of Argentina’s vineyard area) puts world Malbec plantings at roughly 63,000 hectares, conservatively — an older (2023) source implied a larger total; the smaller, more recent, more corroborated figure is used. Not in the OIV world top-10/top-13 table — genuinely smaller in world terms than its wine-list visibility suggests
foodPairing: Complement, classically with steak — Argentina’s beef reputation and Malbec’s soft tannin/dark fruit are a textbook match for red meat’s fat and char

body: Light to medium, extending to fuller/richer in top-tier examples (Wachau’s Smaragd tier)
tannin: None (white grape); some styles show a phenolic bitterness from brief skin contact
acidity: Most consumer sources call it flatly "high," but Tim Gaiser MS’s own professional tasting notes are more precise — "not as high as Riesling," usually "medium-plus." Kept at the more rigorous professional framing
sweetness: Typically dry; a narrower range than Riesling’s, but real — Prädikatswein-level examples can reach genuine sweetness, a minority expression
abv: 11–13.5%, with Smaragd-tier and richer styles needing to reach roughly 13% to fully show varietal character
finish: Medium, described as "energetic" or "refreshing" even in fuller styles
colour: Pale straw with a green tinge, deepening toward gold-green in richer, longer-aged styles
primaryAroma: Green apple, lime, lemon, grapefruit, nectarine — alongside a genuinely prominent vegetal set (green bean, radish, arugula, watercress, asparagus)
secondaryTertiary: White pepper is this grape’s single most famous marker, caused by rotundone — the same compound identified in Syrah/Shiraz. Tim Gaiser’s own professional tasting notes report it in only ~40% of wines he tasted, "not universally found" — most consumer sources overstate it as a guaranteed signature. Richer/aged styles add honey, nuts, smoke
styleRange: Comparable in shape to Riesling’s — a genuine light/simple-to-rich/age-worthy spectrum, tracking Wachau’s own Steinfeder/Federspiel/Smaragd tier system, determined by harvest ripeness and winemaking choice more than a dry-to-sweet axis
confusedWithNote: Closes the loop on both grapes that name GV as their own secondary confusable. Riesling: GV’s white-pepper/vegetal lean vs. Riesling’s petrol/TDN signature and generally higher extract. Sauvignon Blanc: shared high acid and green/vegetal notes, but GV shows a more overtly peppery/nutty character and typically less tropical-thiol lift
globalPrevalence: Austria’s own most-planted grape by a wide margin (~31–32% of national plantings). World total (Kym Anderson’s academic dataset): Austria ~14,376 ha + Slovakia ~1,627 + Czechia ~1,538 + Hungary ~1,381 ≈ 18,900 hectares, roughly 99% of world plantings
foodPairing: Contrast, classically — one of the few wines genuinely recommended alongside notoriously wine-unfriendly vegetables like asparagus and artichoke

body: Medium-plus (Northern Rhône/Syrah) to full/very full (Barossa/Shiraz) — one of the more pronounced body splits between two regional identities of the same grape
tannin: High, firm, fine-grained — consistent across both identities, though Shiraz’s warmer-climate examples often show riper, "bigger"/softer-feeling tannin despite the same underlying level
acidity: Medium to high — Syrah (cooler, Rhône) consistently "brisk"/"vibrant"; Shiraz (warmer, Barossa) consistently softer
sweetness: Dry
abv: 13–15% (Syrah) to 14–15.5% (Shiraz) — Shiraz consistently the higher end
finish: Long
colour: Deep ruby-purple to opaque, inky black when young — one of the darkest of any major red grape, generally darker even than Cabernet Sauvignon
primaryAroma: Blackberry, black cherry, plum (Syrah); riper blueberry, blackberry jam, cooked plum (Shiraz)
secondaryTertiary: Black pepper, caused by rotundone, which this grape produces in greater concentrations than almost any other variety — roughly 1 in 10 people cannot smell it at all. Oak aging (more extensive in Shiraz) adds vanilla, chocolate, sweet spice; with age both identities develop leather, truffle, earth, tobacco
styleRange: The most pronounced same-grape-two-names split researched — genuinely closer to two different wines under one identity than a climate gradient. Syrah (Northern Rhône, cooler): elegant, peppery, floral, restrained oak. Shiraz (Barossa/McLaren Vale, warmer): jammy, riper, higher-alcohol, more extensively oaked, softer tannin despite a similar underlying level
confusedWithNote: Malbec — already covered from the opposite direction, a genuinely weaker, casual-consumer-level pairing. Separately, Petite Sirah is a real name-confusion, not a taste-confusion: despite the similar name, it’s a genetically different grape (a Syrah × Peloursin cross), even more tannic and inky with a denser, chewier texture than true Syrah/Shiraz
globalPrevalence: World’s #6 most-planted wine grape, ~190,000 hectares
foodPairing: Complement — pepper and firm tannin structure classically pair with peppercorn-crusted or char-grilled meats, matching intensity for intensity

body: Medium, ranging light (cool-climate Loire, e.g. Chinon) to full (warm-climate/Bordeaux Right Bank examples)
tannin: Medium, but consistently described as lower/softer/silkier than Cabernet Sauvignon’s
acidity: Medium to high — one of the more acid-forward major reds, a genuinely distinguishing trait relative to its own offspring
sweetness: Dry (vast majority); a genuine minority of late-harvest and ice-wine styles exist
finish: Medium; can age 10–20+ years for top Bordeaux blends or serious single-vineyard Chinon/Bourgueil, though most everyday examples drink young (2–7 years)
colour: Deep purple young, shifting to garnet with age; generally paler than Cabernet Sauvignon
primaryAroma: Raspberry, red plum, sour cherry, red cherry; a distinctive and very consistently reported green/bell pepper note, more pronounced than in its own child, Cabernet Sauvignon
secondaryTertiary: Tobacco, cedar, dried herb, graphite with age; a jalapeño/roasted-pepper/wet-gravel descriptor set specific to Chinon in particular
styleRange: Real, climate-driven: cool-climate Loire (Chinon, Bourgueil, Saumur-Champigny) shows the classic lighter, herbal, red-fruit profile; warmer expressions (parts of Italy, California) show riper dark fruit and a less "green" pepper note, closer in shape to warm-climate Cabernet Sauvignon
confusedWithNote: Cabernet Sauvignon — softer/rounder tannin, more pronounced green pepper, generally lighter body and paler colour. Merlot — a real, documented historical confusion: plantings of Cabernet Franc were literally mistaken for Merlot in vineyards during the early-to-mid 20th century
globalPrevalence: A genuine spread across sources: ~42,500 ha (older baseline) to ~55,000–56,000 ha (more recent figures). Per the conservative-rounding convention, the smaller of the two recent figures is used: ~55,000 hectares
foodPairing: Complement — acidity and moderate tannin pair well with roasted poultry, grilled vegetables, and lighter cuts of red meat; more versatile at the table than either of its higher-tannin offspring

body: Medium — "like Riesling’s acidity meets Chardonnay’s body and texture"
tannin: None (white grape)
acidity: Very high, the grape’s structural backbone across every style from bone-dry to lusciously sweet
sweetness: A genuine dry-to-sweet range comparable in shape to Riesling’s: bone-dry (Savennières, most South African "Steen") through off-dry (Vouvray demi-sec) to intensely sweet, botrytis-affected dessert styles (Quarts de Chaume, Coteaux du Layon)
finish: Long — high acidity gives genuine aging potential across decades, in both dry and sweet styles
colour: Pale straw to medium gold depending on style and age
primaryAroma: Green apple, quince, pear, citrus in drier/cooler styles; peach, ginger, tropical notes in riper/sweeter styles; floral notes throughout
secondaryTertiary: Honey and a distinctive lanolin/wool-like note; botrytis-affected sweet styles add concentrated dried-fruit and honeyed complexity
styleRange: The second "genuinely comparable style range to Riesling" case in this file. Unlike Riesling’s range (climate/harvest-timing-driven within two anchor regions), Chenin’s spreads across many named styles within its two homelands (Loire’s Savennières/Vouvray/Quarts de Chaume vs. South Africa’s more fruit-forward, sometimes oak-aged "Steen") rather than a clean two-region split
confusedWithNote: Riesling — already established from the opposite direction. The tell: Chenin carries the waxy/lanolin note and generally shows more phenolic texture/weight; Riesling’s own signature (especially with age) is the petrol/TDN note, and it typically shows the highest extract of the two
globalPrevalence: 31,200 hectares planted worldwide (2023, Observatoire mondial du Chenin — a dedicated global monitoring body for this grape). South Africa holds roughly half of that global total (sources converge 50–55%; the smaller, 50% figure is used), ahead of France’s own ~30% share
foodPairing: Flexible by style, similar to Chardonnay — dry styles work by contrast (shellfish, goat cheese, salads), off-dry and sweet styles complement spicier or richer dishes where sweetness balances heat or fat

body: The most unanimously-reported same-grape style split in this file — every source checked frames it identically. Pinot Gris (Alsace): fuller-bodied, richer, lush mouthfeel. Pinot Grigio (Italy): light-to-light-medium body, crisp
tannin: None (white grape)
acidity: Medium (Pinot Gris, Alsace) to medium-high (Pinot Grigio, Italy) — the inverse of the body split: the lighter-bodied Italian style carries the higher relative acidity
sweetness: Pinot Grigio (Italy): always dry. Pinot Gris (Alsace): dry to medium-sweet, a real range that doesn’t exist in the Italian identity
abv: 11.5–13.5%, both identities within a similar range
finish: Medium (Pinot Grigio, clean/refreshing) to medium-long (Pinot Gris, more textured)
colour: Pale straw-green (Pinot Grigio) to deeper gold (Pinot Gris) — the grape’s own skin is genuinely pink-gray, and can even be used to make rosé
primaryAroma: Lemon, lime, green apple, white peach (Pinot Grigio, Italy — brighter/citrus-led) vs. pear, peach, honey, sometimes tropical fruit and a touch of spice (Pinot Gris, Alsace — riper/richer)
secondaryTertiary: Pinot Grigio: minimal, typically unoaked, stainless-steel-fermented. Pinot Gris: can show smokiness and spice with age, richer texture, occasional barrel aging in top examples
styleRange: The defining fact of this entry — a colour mutation of Pinot Noir (not a cross, unlike Chardonnay). Pinot Blanc is, in turn, a further mutation of Pinot Gris per one direct source
confusedWithNote: Sauvignon Blanc — a genuinely rich, well-documented pairing (six independent dedicated comparison articles found). The tell: Sauvignon Blanc carries the herbaceous/green methoxypyrazine character (cut grass, bell pepper, gooseberry) Pinot Grigio/Gris lacks, and Sauvignon Blanc’s acidity runs sharper and more assertive
globalPrevalence: Italy alone holds roughly 18,000–19,000 hectares (two sources converge closely: 18,821 and "18,000–19,000"), the world’s largest single-country producer. No exact global total found comparable in rigor to the Italian figure
foodPairing: Contrast (Pinot Grigio’s crisp acidity with light dishes — salads, seafood, grilled vegetables) to complement (Pinot Gris’s fuller body and riper fruit with roasted poultry, pork, creamy sauces, spiced Asian cuisine)

body: Medium to full, occasionally approaching viscous in richer examples
tannin: None (white grape)
acidity: Low to medium — the defining structural trait of this entry, genuinely the lowest acidity of any white grape researched in this file
sweetness: Off-dry is the most commonly reported default style, though genuine dry examples exist (particularly Alto Adige/Italy), and sweet late-harvest/botrytis styles (Vendanges Tardives, Sélection de Grains Nobles) exist at the other end
abv: 11–15%, a genuinely wide but well-sourced range; dry Alsace examples typically run 13–14.5%, late-harvest/SGN styles higher still
finish: Medium to long, particularly in the fuller, richer style
colour: Deep golden yellow, sometimes with copper or pink highlights — a genuine fast recognition cue, tied to the grape’s own pink-red skin
primaryAroma: Lychee is this grape’s single most famous marker, intense enough to identify the wine in a blind tasting from this aroma alone. Rose petal, orange blossom, grapefruit, pineapple, peach, apricot, ginger and other baking-spice notes
secondaryTertiary: Genuinely well-documented aroma chemistry: cis-rose oxide (primary driver, highest odor-activity value among compounds shared with actual lychee fruit), linalool (rose/floral), and geraniol (additional rose/citrus). Botrytis-affected sweet styles add ginger, smoke, incense-like notes
styleRange: Spans dry (increasingly the norm in Alto Adige, some Alsace producers) through the traditional off-dry default to intensely sweet late-harvest/noble-rot styles — but the grape’s low acidity means even the driest examples can read as subjectively "sweeter" than they measure
confusedWithNote: Muscat — both aromatic, both range dry to sweet, both pair with similar cuisines, but Muscat is consistently lighter, more delicate, more fruity/orange-blossom-driven, while Gewürztraminer carries fuller body and a spice-driven profile. Separately, green-skinned Traminer (the non-mutated ancestor) is sometimes mistaken for Gewürztraminer but shows a distinctly less aromatic profile — a naming/lineage confusion, not a genuine taste-alike
globalPrevalence: France (Anderson & Nelgen 2020 academic dataset): 3,320 hectares — used as primary over rounder ~2,800–3,000 ha estimates. Global total, same source: more than 10,000 hectares across the "old world," roughly 2,300 in the "new" — ~12,300+ hectares total, conservatively stated as the lower end of what the source frames as "more than 10,000"
foodPairing: Complement, classically — lush fruit and spice character is the textbook pairing for spicy Asian cuisine and rich, aromatic dishes, since low acidity means it doesn’t cut through richness by contrast

tannin: Low, soft, "velvety" — directly tied to the grape’s thin skin, one of the most consistently low-tannin major reds researched
acidity: A genuine, honest spread across sources — several call it "low," several "medium," one hands-on blind-tasting source specifically describes "medium upper end acidity." Reported as low-to-medium rather than picking one side
sweetness: Predominantly dry, though sweet and semi-sweet styles exist
abv: 13.5–16%, several sources noting "often over 15%" — one of the highest ABV ranges of any grape researched in this file
finish: Medium to medium-plus
colour: Pale ruby, notably lighter than most other major reds researched — directly tied to the same thin skin responsible for its low tannin
primaryAroma: Strawberry, red cherry, raspberry, black cherry
secondaryTertiary: White/black pepper and dried herb (thyme, rosemary) are the most consistently reported secondary markers. One source: "the unmistakable candied fruit roll-up and cinnamon flavor is what gives Grenache away to expert blind tasters." With oak or age: leather, tobacco, citrus rind
styleRange: Climate-driven: Old World examples (Priorat, Châteauneuf-du-Pape) tend more structured and complex with age; New World examples taste riper and more fruit-forward. The traditional "Old World = higher ABV, New World = lower ABV" framing is noted by one source as increasingly unreliable as climates shift
confusedWithNote: Confirms, from the red side, the Tim Gaiser MS "Evil Dwarves" cluster (Pinot Noir, Gamay, Sangiovese, Tempranillo, Grenache, Nebbiolo). No single specific distinguishing tell for a Grenache/Pinot-Noir-or-Sangiovese pairing was independently sourced beyond cluster membership itself — a real, flagged gap rather than an invented tell
globalPrevalence: A genuine decline over time, not source disagreement — from 216,000 ha (twenty years ago) to ~150,000 ha (current), fallen from the world’s most-planted red to 5th among reds. Other sources cite the OIV 2017 Focus figure (163,000 ha, still the more commonly repeated baseline) or Anderson/Adelaide (195,896 ha, 2021). The smaller, most recent, trend-explained figure (~150,000 ha) is used
foodPairing: Complement — soft tannin, high alcohol, dried-herb/pepper character pair well with rich braises and stews (cassoulet, ossobuco) where the wine’s fruit tempers the dish’s heaviness

tannin: Firm to moderate — Puglia/Primitivo trends firmer and grippier; California/Zinfandel trends softer and more "round and generous"
acidity: Moderate
sweetness: Predominantly dry (the once-popular White Zinfandel style is a real, well-known sweet rosé exception)
abv: 13.5–16%, tied to the grape’s uneven within-cluster ripening (some berries raisin while others stay underripe), concentrating sugar and driving high alcohol
finish: Medium to long
colour: Deep violet/purple
primaryAroma: Black cherry, blackberry, dried fig, plum, blueberry compote
secondaryTertiary: Black pepper, cinnamon, clove, chocolate, vanilla (especially in California/barrique-aged examples); with age: tobacco, leather, dried fruit
styleRange: The most rigorously DNA-confirmed same-grape-two-names case researched — UC Davis geneticist Carole Meredith’s 1994 analysis proved identical DNA, later traced (2001) to a near-extinct Croatian variety, Crljenak Kaštelanski/Tribidrag. Puglia/Primitivo trends structured, savory, dry-finishing, higher acid-presenting; California/Zinfandel trends jammier, sweeter-tasting, softer, more oak-forward
confusedWithNote: Answered by the lineage itself rather than a separate taste-alike grape — Primitivo, Zinfandel, Tribidrag, and Crljenak Kaštelanski are one variety under four names across three countries. No additional distinct-grape confusable was independently sourced or needed
globalPrevalence: USA (mostly California/Lodi, ~40% of the state’s Zinfandel crop) holds ~18,551 hectares; Italy (mostly Puglia, ~90% of world Primitivo) holds ~13,896 hectares — a combined ~32,400 hectares across the two dominant countries. A separate source’s "over 40,000 hectares" claim for a narrower California-region set didn’t reconcile cleanly; the smaller, more internally consistent figure is used
foodPairing: Complement — high alcohol and ripe fruit pair with smoky, barbecued, or richly sauced meats; the textbook pairing for American BBQ (Zinfandel) and Italian rustic/grilled dishes (Primitivo)

tannin: Medium to firm, but very consistently described as softer and silkier than Cabernet Sauvignon’s — the same tannin-texture pattern already established for Merlot and Cabernet Franc, its two half-siblings
acidity: Medium to medium-high
sweetness: Dry
finish: Medium; most sources note it is not typically built for long aging (2–3 years is a commonly cited drinking window), a real contrast to Cabernet Sauvignon’s aging reputation
colour: Deep purple-red
primaryAroma: Black cherry, blackberry, raspberry, plum, cassis, alongside a very consistently reported green bell pepper/green pepper note
secondaryTertiary: Chocolate, vanilla, smoke with oak aging; with age: leather, earth. Maipo Valley examples in particular can show a distinctive floral (cherry blossom, hibiscus, rose) and mineral (petrichor, granite-like) character at higher elevations
styleRange: Real but narrower than several other entries — predominantly a warm-climate, ripe, approachable style, without the pronounced regional-identity split seen in Malbec, Syrah/Shiraz, or Primitivo/Zinfandel, since the overwhelming majority of production is concentrated in one country (Chile)
confusedWithNote: Merlot — a genuinely stronger, more consequential case than a typical taste-alike pairing: in 1994, DNA analysis revealed most of what had been sold and planted as "Chilean Merlot" was in fact misidentified Carménère, a real, documented, systematic misidentification confirmed by genetic testing. Also directly confirmed as a half-sibling of both Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot, with Cabernet Franc as its shared parent — Wine Folly groups Carménère, Cabernet Franc, and Cabernet Sauvignon together as all showing pyrazine-driven green pepper character
globalPrevalence: Approximately 95% of world Carménère is grown in Chile; a specific global hectare total comparable in rigor to other entries was not independently located
foodPairing: Complement — moderate tannin and green pepper/herbal character pair with grilled meats and herb-forward sauces (chimichurri, mint, parsley pesto)

tannin: Medium to high — a real, counterintuitive genetics point: both parent grapes (Pinot Noir, Cinsault) are documented as low in colour and tannin, yet Pinotage itself is unusually high in both, "nothing like its progenitors"
acidity: Moderate to medium-high
sweetness: Dry
finish: Medium to long in well-made, quality examples; aging potential has improved significantly as winemaking technique has advanced
colour: Deep ruby-purple, very deeply coloured — inherited from neither low-colour parent, consistent with the tannin/colour paradox
primaryAroma: Red and dark cherry, mulberry, blackberry, plum, black currant
secondaryTertiary: Smoke, dark chocolate, coffee, tobacco, leather, truffle with age. A specific, honestly-reported caveat: a "burnt rubber" or "nail polish remover" (acetone) off-note was historically common in poorly-made examples, tied to fermentation technique rather than an inherent grape trait — top producers have largely eliminated it, but it remains a genuinely useful marker for recognizing a flawed bottle
styleRange: Climate-driven: warmer regions (Paarl, Swartland) produce riper, fuller-bodied, softer-tannined examples; cooler pockets (higher-elevation Stellenbosch, Breedekloof) produce brighter acidity and more lifted red fruit, with one source noting a resemblance to cool-climate Syrah or even Gamay
confusedWithNote: This entry inverts the usual pattern — the "confusion" is about the name, not the taste. Multiple sources directly warn the name invites a false assumption of tasting like Pinot Noir ("It is easy to assume they taste alike. Not true" — Wine Folly, stated directly), when the flavor profile bears little resemblance to either parent grape
globalPrevalence: 6,585.21 hectares in South Africa per SAWIS (South African Wine Industry Information & Systems), cross-confirmed identically across three independent sources including WSET’s own educational blog — "nearly all global plantings," roughly 6–7% of South Africa’s total vineyard area
foodPairing: Complement — smoky, tannic structure pairs with roasted or smoked meats and BBQ; the Cinsault-derived heritage also gives it particular compatibility with Mediterranean vegetables (peppers, aubergine)

tannin: High — consistently and specifically described as "thick-skinned," "grippy," "tight," tied directly to the grape’s genuinely thick skin
acidity: Medium to medium-high
sweetness: Dry
finish: Long — the grape’s dense tannin structure requires genuine bottle age to soften, giving well-made examples real aging potential
colour: Deep, opaque purple — one of the most deeply coloured grapes researched, tied to its thick skin
primaryAroma: Blackberry, blueberry, black plum, black currant
secondaryTertiary: Black pepper, violet, rose, smoke, gravel — and a genuinely distinctive "meaty" or "gamey" aroma when young, specifically flagged as something that "can be mistaken for wine faults" but is a genuine varietal trait rather than always a flaw. With age: truffle, leather, dried fruit
styleRange: Real, climate and region-driven: Southern France (Bandol especially, where the grape is "king") produces the most structured, savory, herb-inflected style; Spain (as Monastrell, its dominant regional name there) produces powerful, full expressions; US examples (California, Washington) trend less tannic and more spice/game-forward
confusedWithNote: Answered by a same-grape-multiple-name situation rather than a taste-alike pairing — Mourvèdre (the dominant international name), Monastrell (Spain), and Mataró are the same grape. "Mourvèdre" is overwhelmingly the more commonly used name in English-language wine writing. No additional distinct-grape taste-confusable was independently sourced
globalPrevalence: Less than 190,000 acres worldwide (approximately 77,000 hectares), with Spain holding the large majority at over 150,000 acres (approximately 61,000+ hectares)
foodPairing: Complement — high tannin and umami-forward gamey character pair with rich, fatty, umami-heavy foods (beef short ribs, pork shoulder, mushroom dishes)

body: Light to medium, with fuller expressions from some regions outside Piedmont’s classic zones (Oltrepò Pavese noted specifically) — a real, honestly-reported spread
tannin: Low — the single most consistently and emphatically reported trait of this entry, described across virtually every source as "soft," "gentle," "smooth," "light"
acidity: Very high — "crackling," "juicy," "zippy," "mouth-watering." One source calls this combination of high acid and low tannin "the giveaway" for identifying the grape
sweetness: Dry
abv: 11.5–14%, with specific regulatory minimums (Barbera d’Asti: 11.5% minimum; Barbera d’Asti Superiore: 12.5% minimum)
finish: Short to medium in everyday styles; longer in oak-aged Superiore-level examples
colour: Deep ruby, near-black — a genuine colour-vs-structure paradox: the near-black colour comes from dark staining pigments in the skin, independent of the light-bodied, low-tannin structure the wine actually shows on the palate
primaryAroma: Dark cherry, sour cherry, strawberry, plum, blackberry
secondaryTertiary: Violet, lavender, dried leaves, incense, anise with age or in more serious expressions; vanilla, nutmeg, toast, cocoa from oak, common in Superiore-level and Barbera d’Alba examples
styleRange: Real and two-tiered by regulation: everyday, fresh, unoaked Barbera d’Asti versus oak-aged, longer-macerated Barbera d’Asti Superiore and the more structured Barbera d’Alba. Documented since the 13th century — "almost 1000 years older than Cabernet Sauvignon" per one direct comparison
confusedWithNote: Dolcetto (not a full entry here) — a well-documented regional-confusable pairing. The tell is structural: Barbera is high-acid/low-tannin; Dolcetto is directly stated as low-acid, its defining trait, with firmer tannin than Barbera despite its "sweet" name (which references low acidity, not sugar). Explicitly confirmed as NOT genetically related to Nebbiolo, Dolcetto, Freisa, or Grignolino despite all being grown in the same region
globalPrevalence: Approximately 13,908 hectares in Piedmont specifically (~30% of the region’s total vineyard area), Italy’s third most-planted grape (after Sangiovese and Montepulciano) at the turn of the 21st century. A second source’s larger figure (~50,000 ha) didn’t reconcile cleanly; the smaller, more specifically-sourced figure is used
foodPairing: Complement to contrast, genuinely flexible — high acidity cuts through fatty and creamy dishes while low tannin and juicy fruit make it broadly food-compatible; one of the most food-versatile reds in Italian wine

body: Light to medium, with a real climate-driven spread toward fuller/riper in warmer sites and lower-yield examples
tannin: Low — very consistently described as "soft," "plush," "faint," "melted"; one direct comparison to Gamay names this exact trait as a shared feature
acidity: Medium to high — "bright," "zippy," "tart," a defining structural trait alongside its low tannin
sweetness: Dry (overwhelming majority); a real minority rosé style exists
abv: 12–13.5% — the grape tends to ripen to a natural ceiling around 13.5% regardless of how much longer it hangs, unlike grapes whose ABV keeps climbing the longer they’re left on the vine
finish: Short to medium in everyday/fruity styles; longer in more serious, lower-yield, sometimes oak-aged examples
colour: Deep ruby to purplish-red
primaryAroma: Cherry (specifically morello/black cherry in riper examples), raspberry, cassis, red and dark berry fruit
secondaryTertiary: Black pepper is the most consistently reported secondary marker; more serious examples add earthy, mineral, tobacco, bay-leaf notes; light oak spice in barrique-aged styles
styleRange: Real and two-directional: light, fresh, fruit-forward "picnic-table" styles (the more common expression) versus more serious, structured, sometimes oak-aged, age-worthy examples from restricted yields
confusedWithNote: Gamay (not a full entry here) — both light-to-medium-bodied, soft-tannined, high-acid reds with a similar bright red-fruit profile, one source drawing the comparison in specific matching detail. Separately, Wine Folly directly describes Zweigelt’s style as evoking Pinot Noir — a real, sourced comparison, and a nice indirect connection back to Pinot Noir’s own confused-with pairing (also Gamay)
globalPrevalence: A well-converged cluster of figures (5,940 to 6,585 hectares). The Austrian Wine industry body’s own 2023/24 statistics report gives 5,940 hectares, 13.4% of Austria’s total vineyard area — Austria’s own most-planted red grape and second-most-planted grape overall (after Grüner Veltliner). Per the conservative-rounding convention, this smaller, most recent, most authoritative figure is used
foodPairing: Complement — soft tannin, bright acidity, and light body make it a genuinely versatile, food-friendly red; suits barbecue, grilled sausage, and casual summer fare

tannin: Low — consistently described as "fine," "restrained," "supple"; several sources directly compare it as even softer than Pinot Noir’s own low tannin
acidity: Medium-high to high — consistently and specifically reported as higher than Pinot Noir’s own acidity, a real, repeated comparative fact
sweetness: Dry (all still and sparkling styles); any perceived sweetness in Champagne comes from dosage decisions in production, not the grape itself
abv: 10–11.5% — the lowest ABV range of any grape researched across all five tranches
finish: Short to medium; most sources note limited aging potential relative to Pinot Noir or Chardonnay, exactly why it’s typically blended rather than bottled as a 100% varietal Champagne
colour: Lighter than Pinot Noir
primaryAroma: Tart cherry, pomegranate, raspberry, blueberry, strawberry, rose petal
secondaryTertiary: Mushroom and earthy notes appear but consistently less pronounced than in Pinot Noir itself; a distinctive rustic, sometimes smoky character and floral spice notes are more characteristic of Meunier specifically
styleRange: A real viticultural role rather than a stylistic range: buds later and ripens earlier than Pinot Noir, giving better frost and cold-weather resistance, why it dominates the colder, north-facing sites of the Marne Valley that Pinot Noir and Chardonnay struggle to ripen consistently. A small but real minority of still red and rosé wines exist outside the blending role, and single-varietal Meunier Champagnes have grown in number recently
confusedWithNote: Gamay (not a full entry here) — a genuinely satisfying closing connection to Pinot Noir’s own lineage: two independent sources directly compare Pinot Meunier to Gamay ("more quaffable Pinot Noir... more similar to Gamay"), the same grape already established as Pinot Noir’s own confused-with pairing — two different members of the same lineage independently converging on the same comparison
globalPrevalence: France holds approximately 80% of world Pinot Meunier plantings, at 12,130 hectares (2016 figure, cross-confirmed identically across four independent sources); within Champagne specifically, roughly 30–40% of the region’s own plantings
foodPairing: Complement — low tannin and bright fruit suit roast poultry, mushroom dishes, and creamy sauces, similar in shape to Pinot Noir’s own food-pairing profile, reflecting the shared lineage

tannin: None (white grape)
acidity: High — described consistently and vividly as "vibrant," "bright," a genuinely defining structural trait
sweetness: Dry to off-dry, with a genuinely useful labeling correction: the DOC-regulated "Extra Dry" category is, confusingly, not the driest style — it is actually off-dry, sitting between the drier "Brut" and the sweeter "Dry"/"Demi-Sec" categories
abv: 8.5–12.5% — 8.5% is the DOC-mandated minimum permitted ABV for Prosecco, among the lowest floors of any grape researched in this file
finish: Short to medium; most Glera wines are made for immediate, youthful consumption, not extended aging
colour: Straw yellow, pale
primaryAroma: Green apple, pear, white peach, with floral notes (honeysuckle, acacia blossom, elderflower); at higher-altitude, lower-yield sites, a genuine mineral/saline finish can develop
secondaryTertiary: Minimal by design — a deliberately neutral-flavored grape; the Charmat/Martinotti tank-fermentation method used for virtually all Prosecco is specifically chosen because it preserves this fresh, fruit-forward primary character rather than adding the yeasty/bready secondary notes traditional bottle-fermentation would
styleRange: Real but narrower than several other entries — virtually all production is sparkling (spumante) or semi-sparkling (frizzante), with only a small minority of still (tranquillo) wines under IGT designations. The DOC/DOCG hierarchy provides the real quality range: Prosecco DOC (large-volume, flatland) versus Conegliano Valdobbiadene DOCG (steep hillside terraces, controlled yields, genuine depth and minerality)
confusedWithNote: Answered by a genuine, consequential naming/legal confusion rather than a taste-alike pairing with a different grape. In 2009, the EU officially renamed the grape variety from "Prosecco" to "Glera," specifically to protect "Prosecco" as a geographic designation of origin rather than a grape name any producer anywhere could use. "Glera" is now the correct varietal name within Italy and the EU; some New World producers, not bound by the same rules, continue using "Prosecco" as if it were a grape name
globalPrevalence: The Prosecco DOC growing zone is most consistently reported at approximately 28,100 hectares (converging closely with a rounder ~30,000 figure elsewhere); one outlier source’s claim of "exceeding 41,000 hectares nationwide" was not corroborated and reads as either a different measure or an overstatement — the smaller, more consistently-corroborated figure is used
foodPairing: Contrast — high acidity and effervescence are the textbook match for salty, fried, or briny foods (seafood antipasti, fritto misto, prosciutto), cutting through richness rather than mirroring it

body: Light to medium-plus; sweeter and fortified styles can become fuller
tannin: None (white grape)
acidity: Medium to good — honestly and consistently reported as not particularly high relative to other aromatic whites in this file, balanced instead by real sugar/flavor concentration when yields are controlled
sweetness: The widest style range of any grape researched across all five tranches — genuinely spans dry, off-dry, sweet sparkling (Moscato d’Asti), and fortified/vin doux naturel, a still-to-sparkling-to-fortified range as well as a sweetness axis
abv: 5–15%+ — the widest ABV range of any grape in this file, from Moscato d’Asti’s legally-capped 5.5% maximum at the low end to standard dry-table-wine and fortified-wine ranges at the high end
finish: Short in sweet sparkling styles (built for immediate, fresh drinking); longer in serious dry or fortified examples
colour: Pale lemon in dry/sparkling styles; deep amber in fortified examples
primaryAroma: The single most distinctive, most-repeated defining trait of this entire tranche: multiple independent sources directly state this grape is "almost the only grape whose wine actually smells and tastes like grapes." Beyond the grapey core: rose petal, orange blossom, jasmine, peach, citrus, and a musky, slightly animal-like note in some expressions
secondaryTertiary: Genuinely well-documented aroma chemistry: the signature perfume is driven by linalool and geraniol — the same two compounds central to Gewürztraminer’s own aroma — plus nerol and citronellol. Fortified/aged styles add honey, nutmeg, and oxidative spice notes
styleRange: The widest range in this file, spanning production method (still, sparkling, fortified) as well as sweetness — see Sweetness above
confusedWithNote: Directly checked against, and confirming, Gewürztraminer’s own forward reference: "lighter, more delicate, and more fruity/orange-blossom-driven" by comparison to Gewürztraminer’s fuller body and spice-driven profile. No additional distinct-grape confusable was independently sourced beyond this comparison
globalPrevalence: A genuine scope ambiguity, reported honestly rather than resolved by picking one number. France’s own figure converges around approximately 7,000–7,540 hectares. A commonly-cited "~45,000 hectares globally" figure exists but is explicitly caveated by its own source as covering "all Muscat à Petits Grains types," potentially including genetically distinct family members (Muscat of Alexandria, Muscat Ottonel, colour mutations), not cleanly isolable to this specific variety. Spain’s own figure for "Moscatel de Grano Menudo" is 21,902 hectares (2015). Honest position: France ~7,000+ ha, Spain ~21,900 ha, with a genuinely uncertain broader-family global total
foodPairing: Contrast to complement depending on style — dry versions pair by contrast with savory dishes; sweet sparkling and fortified versions classically complement fruit-based desserts and pair well with spiced dishes

tannin: None (white grape)
acidity: Very high — the single most consistently and emphatically reported defining trait of this grape across every source checked
sweetness: Dry
abv: Genuinely bimodal by end use: 8–9% ABV specifically for Cognac base wine (deliberately low, since alcohol is built up through distillation, not fermentation), versus a more standard table-wine range for still Trebbiano wines made to be drunk as wine rather than distilled
finish: Short to medium; wines are made for immediate freshness, not extended aging, on either side of the France/Italy naming split
colour: Pale yellow
primaryAroma: Apple, citrus, lemon, grapefruit, subtle tropical notes, with herbal undertones in cooler-climate examples
secondaryTertiary: Minimal by design — the single defining fact of the entry: a deliberately, famously neutral flavor profile, prized specifically because it is neutral, so it doesn’t compete with what’s built on top of it (a blend’s other components in Italy; the spirit’s own developing character through Cognac’s extended oak aging in France)
styleRange: Genuinely climate-driven: cooler climates preserve acidity and produce more restrained, herbal examples; warmer climates enhance fruit ripeness and body. The deeper structural range is really about end use — light blending/base-wine component (the overwhelming majority) versus, in a genuine minority of quality-focused Tuscan and Abruzzese examples, wines of real, serious depth
confusedWithNote: No taste-alike confusable was found, and that absence is itself worth stating directly rather than forcing a pairing — likely a direct consequence of the grape’s own defining neutrality. A grape whose entire character is the deliberate absence of a distinctive signature has little for another grape to be confused with; if anything, the "confusion" risk runs the other way — a taster is more likely to fail to identify it at all than to mistake it for something else
globalPrevalence: World total 111,000 hectares, ranking #10 globally among wine grape varieties (OIV Focus 2017, fetched directly from the report itself). France and Italy’s own national totals (approximately 90,000 ha and 55,000 ha respectively) are real national subtotals that, combined with smaller plantings in Portugal and elsewhere, sum to the OIV’s 111,000-hectare world total
foodPairing: Flexible, light-touch — high acidity and deliberate neutrality make it a genuinely unobtrusive food partner, working with salads, light seafood, and oily fish (sardines specifically named) without imposing its own character

tannin: Medium to high, with a texture repeatedly described as smoother and more approachable than its tannin level alone would suggest — a texture-not-just-quantity pattern already familiar from Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Carménère, and Malbec
acidity: Medium to medium-high
sweetness: Dry
finish: Medium to long in serious examples (Riserva-level, longer macerated); shorter in everyday, fruit-forward bottlings
colour: Deep ruby to inky purple — among the most deeply coloured grapes researched across all five tranches, comparable to Malbec’s and Mourvèdre’s own deep colour
primaryAroma: Dark cherry, blackberry, plum, blueberry
secondaryTertiary: Black pepper, dried herb, licorice; leather and tobacco with age; vanilla and baking spice where oak is used
styleRange: Real and quality-tier-driven: everyday, fresh, stainless-steel Montepulciano d’Abruzzo versus more structured, longer-macerated, sometimes oak-aged Riserva-level examples from top producers (Valentini and Emidio Pepe are the two most consistently cited benchmark names)
confusedWithNote: The name itself, not the taste, is the real confusion here — and the most consequential of this file’s name-driven confusions, since it involves two completely different wines, not just a variant name for the same thing. "Montepulciano" the grape (this entry, mostly Abruzzo) is unrelated to Vino Nobile di Montepulciano, a wine from the Tuscan hill town of Montepulciano made predominantly from Sangiovese (locally called Prugnolo Gentile) — the names are identical but the wines share no grape in common
globalPrevalence: Italy’s third most-planted red grape variety (behind Sangiovese and ahead of Barbera at the turn of the 21st century), concentrated overwhelmingly in Abruzzo; a precise current hectare figure comparable in rigor to this file’s other entries was not located with confidence
foodPairing: Complement — full body and dark fruit character suit hearty, rustic Italian dishes (grilled meats, ragù, aged cheeses)
